title: The Witness
text: I entered the world, and there were some terminals that you go to to solve a puzzle.  You walk up to the screens, and the puzzles appear on the monitor in the game. To solve these puzzles, you have a starting point and drag a line like "Snake" along a grid to the end point.  Every puzzle has this base.  The rules change, but the game does a good job of letting you know what the rules are without explicitly stating them. There was a good looking world around, but I didn't seem to interact much with it, only the puzzle screens.  The world is featured prominently in the screenshots on the store page.  The puzzles are the opposite of the beautiful world; they are literally just dots and lines.  And there isn't a single puzzle featured in the screenshots Some of the puzzles required thought and were well made.  However, you walk from screen to screen, and that seems to be it.  It isn't like Braid where you interact with the level. I solved something like 100 puzzles and got bored.  I opened up a walkthrough on Youtube and scanned through parts in the middle and end.  It looks like it is just more puzzle screens, so I gave up on the game.  If this was a flash game (which it could be), it would have held my attention for about 10 minutes.  I gave this game more of a chance because I figured there was more to it.  This would be a real letdown for the full price, but since I got it as part of the freedom bundle, I got this and other games with all of the money going to the ALCU and other orgs.  Props to the developer for that, but I cannot recommend this game.

title: The Witness
text: "You wake up, alone, on a strange island full of puzzles that will challenge and surprise you. You don't remember who you are, and you don't remember how you got here, but there's one thing you can do: explore the island in hope of discovering clues, regaining your memory, and somehow finding your way home." They got the alone on a strange island part right.  The problem is, the puzzles are on these incongruous pads littered all over the landscape.  You draw a colored line from the round start pad to the exit.  Now draw it while separating these colored dots from those colored dots, or while covering dots on the path.  Or something else.  There's literally nothing to explain any of this to you - you figure it out by trial and error. Some of the pads are pretty self-explantory.  Others you sit there scratching your head and wondering what on earth you're intended to do.  Once you've figured one type of pad out, you'll easily plow through others of the same type... but that won't be any help at all with the weird unmarked hexagon pad that you were scratching your head about.  Now I enjoy a good puzzle as much as most people, but somehow I'm not getting my jollies when I'm drawing lines on pads to get power to more pads so I can draw lines on them - it's just dull. In the two hours I spent as of this review, I've wandered around a few different areas and completed one.  My reward for this completion was a laser pointing way off into the distance.  What does the laser do?  Why does this island have hundreds of panels devoted to drawing lines, simply to power it and presumably other lasers?  Maybe you'll get some sort of plot exposition at the end of the game, but you certainly won't for the rest of it.  You're alone on a strange island, deal with it.

title: The Witness
text: In many ways I don't feel qualified to write about this game. First of all I cheated. Out of the 300 puzzles I cleared to finish this game (out of about 700, I believe) I had to look up solutions for maybe 5-10% of that. Therein lies the shame, and the act of playing into the developer's hand of being an illogical being, driven by comfort rather than intellectual curiosity. Games have long conditioned us to look for help if we are stuck and to fully resort to the helping hand in such a predicament; this instead of our own ability or logic. Realizing this you are swiftly thrown into discomfort, playing The Witness. Because the game has a logic to it, but you can only rely on yourself to figure out the system in play. The mechanics are obscured by non-knowledge, but that's what makes this game so unique, and what constitutes its elegance and beauty as a game. I can't say that I have played a game that has required as much of me as The Witness. It requires trust and dedication, trusting that the game is working properly, that when you do not know something, that is what the game intends. And the only way a game can pull something like that off is with having absolutely impeccable game-design. There can't be any tricking of the player, in any sense. Blow mentions in an interview that he does not want to trick the player into feeling smart, which he never does with this game, but more so I think it's important to not trick the player into feeling dumb. Once a player start to doubt his or her own ability to solve something due to a lack of information, it's over. But even in this regard I think that The Witness succeeds in making the player feel like the answer of any puzzle lies within the game itself. My problems mainly arose when I knew that I didn't know, because I knew I disregarded certain places of the game where I felt like I couldn't grasp the logical rule-sets, or where I couldn't get over the leaps of logic even after I looked up solutions for certain puzzles. I conceded, there was no real trust in my own ability. That and my impatience lead to a certain mistrust of the game. But with this view back on myself, I see that the problem is not with the game-design, it is with me. Because I can't stress this enough, this game is elegant in a way I have never seen before. It is a self-sufficient game. It's cyclical, it is an exercise in the Nietzschean return. Repetition of fleeting activities, grasping at shadows of pleasure, the attempt to make something out of nothing, personal progression, are all parts of this game. Narratively, visually and according to the mechanics we are witnessing the eternal return of our activities as human beings, our purpose as lifeforms. The Witness adumbrates a great deal of humanity, an intimacy that becomes so much closer despite the distance required when viewing ourselves existentially. The Witness is this incredible holistic experience that encapsulates the art of game-design without profusion. It is clinical, precise and executed perfectly, which you will notice with enough trust in the game-design and with enough appreciation for game-creation. At the heart of this game – what is really the core of this experience, to me – is what goes on in your head, and what this game requires of you as a person; as a mind among minds, as a human being with intelligence. What I noticed fairly early on was my desperate need to vocalize the principles that each puzzle was run by. I had to vocalize this intuitively logical puzzle, just to wrap my head around what was required. This is not something I've ever really experienced before in games, and I was surprised to see it come out in a medium that is not often lauded for its intellectuality. Because this process of vocalizing or making conscious and intuitive form of intelligence puts it in the view of self-conscious scrutiny. This is a quality that can be very valuable for people in general, and in its own way The Witness has the possibility of teaching it. What I referred to earlier in terms of elegance, was in regards to the game-design, puzzle-design and the comportment of this game. This elegant restraint and non-compromise with the idiocy of the gamer's conditioned need for help, bleeds into its over all presentation. There is almost no music or extravagant sound-design, but runs the gamut of beautifully suiting each situation with an aural atmosphere that never feels empty nor mawkishly musical. It's this portrayal of life as “doing”, as functionality and concreteness. Every sound has its place, it springs out of the movement of the player and has a natural flow to it that in accordance with the visuals manage to structure a believable holistic world. Every facet goes with the theme of an encapsulation of being within something very fleeting, finding familiarity in a world that you're thrown into and out of, at least for the moment being. While this is the attempt, at least seemingly, it is hindered by self-hatred spawned out of inability. That is, however, limited to the dynamics of the individual, to what is deemed subjective. The Witness succeeds in creating a stimulating world in all senses of that word, to all senses. In terms of visuals, I struggle to think of a game I think is more beautiful than this. In terms of composition, level design, environment, colors and lighting, it's out of this world, but more worldly than most games. There is this marriage between naturalism and human influence, between nature and machine, between natural colors and vibrant neon, between vocalized LOGIC AND VISUAL CUES. When I get some time I am going to revisit this game with a fresh mind. I am not going to look up solutions and I am going to wholly dedicate myself to this experience. The Witness is incredible, and unless this game spawns a trend of games following in its footsteps, we will most likely not see anything quite like this in a very long time. I'm the type of person to be subjugated under things I consider to be more intelligent than me, and this game falls under that category. That means I am naturally inclined to praise it, solely due to the fact of it being “above me”. I have yet to master this game, even though I have beaten it, I don't feel like I have beaten it, and I that alone makes me impressed. I do not feel finished with the game, I couldn't happily move on from this game. Because I know there is more to it. I know there is more to learn and that curiosity will drive me back to this experience. And I think that is special. Especially special enough to warrant a recommendation. I believe this is a game where the more time you dedicate to it the better it gets and the more fulfilling it becomes. It simulates and portrays the essence of human – even personal – progression in so many ways and so perfectly, and it has so many moments of beauty and immense respect before the creator. If If I were to inhabit this world as my only existence I'd bow down in eternal love for its creator. I respect this creation and most of all I appreciated the experience. It was okay.

title: The Witness
text: The Witness manages to be less, much less than the sum of its parts. The game seems to be a collection of puzzles, so these are the "parts". To me these puzzles seemed interesting, smart and original, but then again im not a big fan of puzzles so what seemed smart and original to me could be silly old stuff for somebody more puzzle oriented. To sum it up, i really enjoyed the puzzles i encountered so far and the way to solve them but...as a videogame this thing is an atrocity, a heresy, an insult. Its a shame to see so much potential go to waste because the developer couldnt afford a game designer. They packaged chef d'oeuvre puzzle candies in a moldy cardboard box full of grease stains and with some flies and worms for good measure. There is nothing wrong with puzzles but, when you are thrown into a semi open world environment that is full of potential puzzles that might or might not be solvable at that point, its way too easy to oversee a puzzle that might be doable and insist on doing one that is undoable, not to mention a lot of pointless tracking and backtracking through environments that are not very pretty but feel very empty. Its a shame that a game that had the potential to be an exercise for the mind, turned into an exercise in patience, perseverence and  resistance to tedium, for the sole reason of poor design. Once i get to a series of puzzles that are doable, i finish them almost without effort and i have to admit i have some satisfaction from that but....too much time wasted finding the puzzles, more time finding a puzzle than solving it....not good. The way the puzzles are presented to the player is lacking, and there is a lack of purpose for the whole thing. Yeah ok im solving these puzzles and i feel good and smart but...why am i doing this? Just to prove myself i can do it? Cuz it sure aint fun. All this game needed to be a masterpiece, was a halfway decent game designer. The developer created a very nice set of puzzles (imho), but they completely failed to implement these puzzles into a coherent and satisfying game. To sum it up, i consider the puzzles to be superb but the implementation to be awful. As a rather unusual and possibly satisfying puzzle experience (if you are very resistant to tedium), i would give it a big thumbs up, but as a videogame, a huge thumbs down, and since this was sold as a videogame...i can only give it a thumbs down. Also worth mentioning is that no matter how you look at it, this product is not worth the asking price, since not only it is not a fancy A+ game, but its hardly a game at all. Only got this in my collection because im subscribed to humble monthly, but if i paid the asking price for this game, i would be refunding with a rage.

title: The Witness
text: Excellent puzzles, great atmosphere, great game. To elaborate a bit: I like puzzles, but too often puzzles aren't "fair".  You solve them by bashing them, by trying a bunch of stuff or you happen into an answer - but you groan because you didn't actually do any interesting thinking, or the correct "answer" isn't better than others you've tried.  Out of hundreds of puzzles in Witness, there was only 2 or 3 that I didn't like.  Almost all were fair and many were a real solid level of difficulty. And a few were just amazing: difficult but fair, requiring a combination of lateral thinking, cleverness and deduction.  I really like puzzles where you can solve them through a series of small realizations, rather than just finding the "whole answer" all at once - and that was a core feature here.  There was some absolutely beautiful moments in this game. Overall: a puzzle game that belongs in a very short list with classics like Braid or Portal.

title: Thief™ II: The Metal Age
text: Thief II The Metal Age is easily one of the best games of all time and the pinnacle of not only stealth in video games, but level design and story telling. I may be in the minority in saying that I prefer both the original and Deadly Shadows more, but goddamn if this isn't a worthy successor in every way, continuing the series and building upon the world that you helped shape by the end of the last game. ++The sound design in this game is phenomenal. The propogation engine, the voice acting, how it effects gameplay, everything is just at the highest standard possible which is to say totally unmatched. ++The cutscenes in this game are, again, and I'll be repeating this a few times, totally unmatched within video games as a whole ++The atmosphere is extraordinary, even if it isn't as strong as Dark Project or Deadly Shadows ++Levels can take an hour or more to complete and are totally rewarding the whole way through ++The sneaking is just plain fun +Graphics are a noticable improvement over the Dark Project more so in consistency and art style then technical acheivement. +Using Tafferpatcher, I couldn't ask for smoother performance on modern systems +Levels are huge, but not for the sake of being huge +The addition of officially marked secrets is awesome +A lot of the new equipment is really cool +I've always liked the animations in these games, but some people seem to think they've aged really badly +-The soundtrack by Eric Brosius was made to be more musical than ambiant and it doesn't work nearly as well. It's in no way bad though. -+The Life of the Party is just disappointing, but I guess it's not its fault it got hyped so much. Plus, it's not bad by any stretch of the imagination. +-What the hell are the point in vine arrows? I used them like once for metal surfaces the whole game. -One level is turned into two which is utterly lazy and unenjoyable considering how the level wasn't even that good the first time -Movement seems to glitch on surfaces more than the first game which is quite frustrating -Physics tied to framerate (60FPS) -Mantling works 40% of the time and is 90% the reason I get caught. I don't know what happened from Gold to 2 to have it be so frustrating. -If you're crouching in pitch black, not moving and an enemy isn't already alerted to you they can walk into you without getting alerted. I've had multiple occurences of that happening and them getting stuck on me for a couple of minutes. It's just silly. -Bit of a glitch fest -The storyline is only half as good as Thief the Dark Project or Deadly Shadows --The last 3 missions are beyond disappointing. After 3+ playthroughs I still have never once had the will power to finish the final level no matter how hard I try. The two before it are the worst in the game besides it and it really doesn't help that both levels are exactly the same in layout with terrible level design. ---I honestly find the level design to be a large step back from the original. There's a reason the entirety of Follow the Courier's concept was only a tiny section of Assassin's back in Gold. A lot of levels are tedious, repetitive and not great in the replayability department. This being said, it's not terrible, it's just very disappointing. Sound: 10/10 Graphics: 8/10 Gameplay: 9/10 Content/Replayability: 7.5/10 Overall: 8.5/10 Awards: Runner-Up Game of the Year - 2000 On my first playthrough, I found it hard to decide whether I liked Gold or 2 more. title: Thief™ II: The Metal Age
text: Thief II: The Metal Age sets the high water mark for stealth gaming.  Bar none.  No game before or since can compare to the immersiveness of this game and it's fine-tuned mechanics.  It manages to mix the fantasy, strategy and adventure aspects of the first with a more prescient storyline than the first Thief game.  The first game was an excellent stealth game that occasionally drifted too far into Tomb Raider territory with it's platformy style missions, devious traps and creature threats.  The fact that Eidos was the publisher of both Thief and Tomb Raider, and that one of the missions had you raiding an underground tomb frought with booby traps and monsters, ought to tell you something.  Thief 2 , thankfully, focuses on the strengths of the stealth system and makes that the core of the game and not just an aspect of it.  That's not to say you won't be jumping across ravines and encountering creatures, but the heist-pulling, pick-pocketing and blackjacking really comes into thier own in Thief 2.  I've read that the developers created the missions of the first game to suit the plot, while the missions of the second were produced first with the plot retrofitted.  In any case, the levels are larger and more complex than the first. The graphics had gotten a slight bump from the first game with higher poly models, better texturing and weather effects.  They even added dithering to the hardware renderer, which was a nice addition.  It did have the effect of dampening the deep shadows that were such a part of the first game, but it generally made the game more pleasing to the eye. The sound design is, again, excellent.  Sound propagation is one of the core facets of gameplay.  Listening to footsteps draw near or fade into the distance allow you to judge from your hiding place in the shadows whether or not you can risk stepping into lit areas.  Leaning against doors to listen to conversations or the presence of sounds in the next room allow you to determine if opening a door is wise or not.  Sound is fundamental to this game.  You will not be able to play this game successfully while blasting Megadeth or Slayer.  Just not happening.  And that's one of the things that makes this game so damn immersive.  You are literally concerned with the environment both visually and aurally at all times.  It sucks you in. There are some new gadgets in this game.  Garrett lost an eye in the first game, and that has been replaced by a mechanical eye that can zoom in and out like a telescope.  A new object called the Scouting Orb allows you to take a peak over walls or around corners without exposing yourself.  There are also new potions and a new arrow:  the vine arrow.  Similar to the rope arrow, but it can "stick" to things rope arrows can't, like metal gratings. The design went from a predominantly dark age style steampunk in Thief 1 to a predominantly Victorian era style steampunk in Thief 2, in much of it's architecture.  Actually, art deco also makes an appearance as part of the design of buildings operated by a faction that's new to Thief 2, the Mechanists.   The European old world oozes in these games.  In fact, many of the textures from Thief 1 and Thief 2 were from photos of architecture taken by the developers while vacationing in Europe.   The overall design is pretty immaculate. The first two Thief games share a cult status, along with System Shock2 (uses the same game engine and made by some of the same people), as games of remarkable vision and quality.  They are all lauded as excellent games by the gaming press and continue to make the top # lists.  The gameplay transcends gaming.  To play this game is to embark on an existential and  metaphysical experience.  This game seems to attract a higher-brow gaming audience.  There is a community forum that has been the stomping grounds of its players since the games were released.  They have created hundreds of fan missions to play; you can find it here: Here you can get a community made patch that updates the rendering of the game and allows for some nice effects, like bloom, while also fixing a number of leftover bugs: Here you can get a high resolution patch that updates some models, textures and also adds a numbder of new effects to the game: Here you can read about and find fan missions to play:

title: TimeShift™
text: This game is...eh, ok. Graphics? Fine. Music? Good. Story? Nice! ... ... But what it really made me do, is think. We live our lives, matter/energy, moving in space-time. We are largely at the mercy of matter, energy, and space. Oh, there's gravity, sunlight, electromagnetism, electricity, hot, cold, etc. But our concept of time is always the same: It's moving forward. Tick-tock-tick-tock. None of us can really manipulate time. Make it run slower, or stop it, or even reverse it. Nope, that's not how we live our day-to-day lives. But you know, if you can manipulate time like that, then seriously, we won't be at the mercy of matter, energy, and space so much. We can stop fire from burning, stop electricity from electrocuting, stop ourselves from plunging into water. Suppose you are in a collapsing bridge. It falls, you along with it. Reverse time to the point that it is still standing. Heck, while time is in reverse, get the heck off that bridge. This game has enough scenarios like that. Sh** if this game can make you re-think your concept of reality, then its a darn good game.

title: TimeShift™
text: TimeShift succeeds in being one of those games where it's required of the player to pay attention to detail if they want to understand the ending. Because the ending can be confusing if you weren't following along with the cutscenes or any of the dialog spoken by Krone during various instances. Before I get into the game itself, a few things you should know if you want TimeShift to run properly on your system: 1. Find the TimeShift.exe in the install folder and change the compatibility to Windows XP (SP3) 2. Find and install patch 1.2 for the game as Steam/Activision only have it updated to 1.0 and you'll have a slew of problems. I'm pretty sure those two cover it, the game will run much more smoothly and won't/shouldn't freeze on any loading screen or when paused. I can't say I enjoyed the overall story in TimeShift, the whole stop a madman from ruining everything in a dystopia seemed rather generic. I did like that the protagonist stays unnamed and has ulterior motives when he jumps into the past to save the future. The gameplay was rather repetitive, running and gunning, going through vast buildings, pushing buttons, sometimes driving, using a turret, climbing up and down ladders. That's pretty much it. The saving grace with the gameplay is the time manipulation ability that comes with the Beta suit that the protagonist has. It's really cool, being able to stop time and seeing rain just frozen in mid air. Or reversing an action if you messed up. Or slowing down time/being able to move really fast. I guess my biggest complaint was how uninspired the story seemed at times. There's hardly any background as you're just thrown into a situation. I would compare the whole situation of a dystopian world and you're the hero to Half Life, but at least in Half Life, there's context given and side characters that explain the situation. The side characters in TimeShift are so minor that I actually thought they were expendable and was surprised when the small crew you're with for a large portion of the game survives. Granted, you're not actually with them; most of the time, they'll stay behind and let you do all the work. At least the graphics are still pretty good. Obviously a bit dated being 8 years old now but the whole world had an atmosphere of 'wow, this place is really falling apart' and added so much to the overbearing dystopia. Sound design was pretty great too. Anyway, while it has a number of flaws, TimeShift still proved to be fun after I got it working. 8/10

text: Have you always wanted to star in your own 70's Euro-toon involving a powerful pair of underwear and a lazer beam that can slice through anything?! Now's your chance.

title: Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers
text: The entire game is based on a single ability: your laser that can cut and slice through pretty much all objects in the scenery. While it's fun at first, it's very limited and all of the whopping 6 levels feel pretty much like you are doing the same thing. The physics are pretty glitchy as well and the controls not very precise, so be prepared for a few frustrating/unavoidable deaths. New levels don't add any new gameplay elements, and the graphics (which are not great looking) aren't varied either, adding to the feeling that all levels are pretty much the same. But then it doesn't even matter because the whole game ends in 2 hours, before it has time to get boring further.

title: Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers
text: Pros: - Comic book art style - Unique laser cutter and grappling hook mechanics - Quirky - Short (doesn't overstay its welcome) - Silly story Cons: - Stiff platforming (think Kingdom Hearts 1) - Lots of accidental deaths Tiny and Big at its best can be a delightful and fresh action platformer. It's weird in a good way which helps to drive the player to progress to see how much weirder it will get. The laser cutter mechanic is unique and fun to use. The downside with this game is mainly its physics. It's a decent physics engine (don't get me wrong). But with an action platformer that depends so much on its physics mechanic, it's to be expected that there will be a lot of cheap accidental deaths. This can cause a great deal of frustration. To remedy this, the developers allowed for a near instant respawn (though you may be placed a few paces back). Another thing is the platforming. It's not terrible but it just feels stiff and imprecise which also allows for frustrating accidental deaths. All in all, I appreciate what the developers tried to create with this indie title. It would be extremely difficult to implement these unique ideas without all of the associated hiccups. If you're into action platformers and you're looking for one that's different from the norm. Check out Tiny and Big. Get it on sale. 7/10

title: Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers
text: Tiny & Big is the antithesis to Minecraft. A game where you can destroy and move giant clumps of rock with a stone cutting laser beam, a grappling hook and a rocket launcher. When I played this, I got a vibe as if I was playing Super Mario 64 again. Must have been the 64 bit graphic design. Or the fact that this game is sort of a collectathon with lots of achievements. This game isn't too impressive in the graphical department, but its makes up with unique and fresh 3D sandbox puzzle environment which I never experienced like this before. Comes with a collection of indie musician tracks from an all time portable radio. Choose your tunes while being a stonecutter. Yes, the game has no enemies whatsoever, some bonus levels are kind of derp and the few boss battles against the one and only other human character are practically all in the same fashion, but this game was made by a small indie studio and should not be scolded for such shortcomings too much. I hope Black Pants Studios will make a follow up to this game with some Coop. If this series gets some polishing and a better publicity it could aspire to be a competitor to Portal! In the meantime, if you are looking for a challenge, consider acquiring this. Its fairly cheap and often on sale. Definitely an enrichment to your steam library.
